name: Tunisia
summary_text: Tunisia criminalises same-sex conduct under Penal Code Article 230, which carries up to three years' imprisonment, and enforcement is active rather than dormant. Article 226 bis on public indecency is applied to gender expression, and enforcement of both provisions falls disproportionately on transgender women. In October 2021 two transgender women were arrested under morality and debauchery provisions.  The scale of the current campaign is documented by Amnesty International on 11 February 2025: at least 84 people, mainly gay men and transgender women, were arrested, arbitrarily detained and prosecuted between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025 on public indecency and morality charges. The arrests took place in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef, so the sweep is national in character rather than confined to one city. A mass conviction on 31 October 2024 imposed prison terms of up to four and a half years; the convictions were upheld on appeal on 5 February 2025, with four people released only after sentence reduction.  Human Rights Watch recorded at least seven men prosecuted for consensual same-sex conduct in two cases over six months in 2016, all convicted under Article 230. Detainees interviewed in those cases reported beatings, forced anal examinations and humiliating treatment by police, which places physical abuse by the security services inside the ordinary arrest process rather than outside it.  Tunisia pledged to the United Nations in 2017 to stop forced anal testing in homosexuality cases while retaining the anti-gay law itself, so the commitment changed examination practice without decriminalising anything. A visitor should not read that pledge as a change in exposure to prosecution.  Legal gender recognition is unsettled and frequently refused. In April 2023 the Tunis Court of First Instance refused recognition to a transgender man, weighing contradictory lower-court judgements, including case No. 12304/2018, and finding no consistent precedent; the question remains unresolved below the Court of Cassation, which makes recognition a court-by-court gamble. Cairo 52 records that gaps persist in legal gender recognition generally.  Custody carries documented identity risk. The Intersection Association reported in November 2024 that transgender women in Tunisian prisons are processed under their former names and birth gender in detention records, arrest processes and court hearings, a systemic refusal of identity from the point of detention onward and a source of continuous suffering inside the prison system. A trans visitor who is detained should expect documents and hearings to use a name and gender marker they do not recognise.

sources.title: Association Shams - enforcement statistics 2016-2019
sources.documents: Scale of enforcement post-2011 revolution: 56 jailed in 2016, 79 in 2017, 127 in 2018, at least 22 arrests as of April 2019; plus 7 Dec 2016 Sousse arrests with forced anal probe and 11 March 2017 eight-month sentences
sources.detail: Cited in text as 'Local LGBTQ association Association Shams has reported that since the Tunisian revolution in 2011, an increasing number of gay men have been being jailed: 127 in 2018, in contrast to 79 in 2017, and 56 in 2016. name: Ukraine
summary_text: Nothing about being trans is criminalised in Ukraine. Legal gender recognition exists, but the procedure is medicalised: the 2016 protocol requires a "transsexualism" diagnosis and psychiatric observation before documents are amended. Against that requirement stands a concrete gain — a Ukrainian court ordered changes to passports and all other documents for two trans people without requiring sterilisation.  Obtaining the diagnosis that unlocks those documents has become harder. ZMINA reported on 28 July 2026 that trans women in Ukraine now face stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers when seeking a diagnosis, and that the difficulty is documentary as much as medical, affecting both the transition procedure and border crossing. Reporting from France 24 in June 2022 already placed Ukraine's trans community in the crosshairs of the war.  Wartime procedure carries the sharpest visitor-facing risk. Gender Stream documents that since martial law began, holders of male gender markers were stopped at the border by the State Border Guard Service, and the organisation helps with processing or reissuing documents for transgender people, including those planning to cross the border legally. Human Rights Watch reported on 15 May 2024 that cross-border networks became critical support for trans women in Ukraine, arranging assessments, diagnoses and the often-humiliating Military Medical Commission confirmation; a Ukrainian activist described the commission's 8am to 8pm operating hours and gatekeeping that turns on a single doctor's statement.  Family recognition is now at risk in draft law. A revised Civil Code draft submitted to Parliament on 22 January 2026 would automatically annul marriages if one spouse undergoes legal sex reassignment, directly targeting trans people's family status. Trans Forum 2026, held in Kyiv in early June 2026, discussed that draft's effect on the transition procedure and whether being trans should ground an exemption from mobilisation.  Protection machinery exists but is thin. Amnesty International reported on 16 May 2013 that Ukraine's government had to legislate against discrimination and violent attacks on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity amid a pervasive climate of homophobia, and that attacks were routinely used as a pretext to deny LGBTI people the right to expression and peaceful public events. The European Parliament put the situation of transgender people in Ukraine amid the Russian invasion on the record in written question E-002018/2022 in June 2022.

sources.title: Constitution of Ukraine, Article 51 (1996)
sources.documents: Defines marriage as a voluntary union between a man and a woman; bars legal recognition of same-sex marriage.
